blocks.title: Background
blocks.content:
Digital health – defined broadly as the systematic application of information and communications technologies (ICT), computer science and data 
to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health 
and wellness (1) – is increasingly being applied as an essential enabler for health service delivery and accountability. Ministries of health (MOHs) have 
recognized the value of digital health as articulated within the World Health Assembly resolution (2) and the Global strategy on digital health (3). 
Li

summary.text: Explains the background to WHO digital adaptation kits, noting that despite investment in digital health, the data and logic in digital tools are often opaque, inconsistent or proprietary and not clearly linked to evidence-based recommendations. It describes the kits as software-neutral, standardised documentation that distils WHO guidance into content for digital tracking and decision-support systems, mapped to standard terminologies such as ICD. It defines digital tracking and decision support and identifies the core WHO family planning guidance documents the kit draws on, such as the medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use.

blocks.title: Objectives
blocks.content:
This DAK focuses on family planning and aims to provide a common language across various audiences – family planning and other programme 
managers, software developers, and implementers of digital systems – to ensure a common understanding of the appropriate health information content 
within a defined health programme area, as a mechanism to catalyse the effective use of these digital systems. The key objectives of the DAK are:
	»
to ensure adherence to WHO clinical, public health and data use guidelines, and facilitate consistency of the health content that is used to inform 
the development

summary.text: States the objectives of the family planning digital adaptation kit: to keep digital tracking and decision-support systems consistent with WHO guidelines, give health and digital teams a shared understanding of content, and supply core data elements and decision logic. It lists the source guidelines, notes that outputs are generic and must be adapted locally, and mentions related kits for antenatal care, HIV and STIs.

blocks.title: Components of a digital adaptation kit
blocks.content:
The DAK comprises eight interlinked components: (1) health interventions and associated recommendations; (2) generic personas; (3) user scenarios; 
(4) business processes and workflows; (5) core data elements; (6) decision-support logic; (7) indicators and performance metrics; and (8) high-level 
functional and non-functional requirements. Table 1 provides an overview of each of the contributing components of the DAK, which this document 
elaborates. All information within the adaptation kit represents a generic starting point, which can then be adapted according to the specific context.
Table

summary.text: Describes the eight interlinked components of a digital adaptation kit, from health interventions and recommendations, personas and user scenarios through workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, indicators and system requirements. A table sets out each component's purpose, outputs and adaptation needs. It also explains the identifier conventions used for data elements, decision tables, indicators and requirements.

blocks.title: Table 1. Components of a digital adaptation kit
blocks.content: The table lists the eight components of the digital adaptation kit (DAK), from health interventions and recommendations to functional and non-functional requirements. For each component it gives a description, its purpose, the outputs it provides and the adaptation needed for a specific context.

blocks.title: How to use this digital adaptation kit
blocks.content:
Target audience
The primary target audience for this DAK is health programme managers within the MOH, who will be working with their digital or health information 
systems counterparts in determining the health content requirements for a family planning DTDS system. The health programme manager is responsible 
for overseeing and monitoring the implementation of the clinical practices and policies for the health programme area, in this case family planning. 
Other stakeholders, including software development teams and implementers in the private sector, will can also benefit from the content in

summary.text: Identifies ministry of health family planning programme managers as the main audience for the kit, working with digital health and information system counterparts and business analysts. It explains how the kit supports collaboration and adaptation to local contexts and notes that client-facing digital tools will be covered in a forthcoming self-care kit.

summary.text: Presents two user scenarios for family planning services: a nurse who registers and counsels a breastfeeding mother during her baby's immunization visit and starts her on progestogen-only pills, and a 16-year-old who seeks help after a condom slipped. The adolescent scenario shows confidential registration, a HEADSS assessment, emergency contraception and dual protection with combined pills and condoms, with SMS follow-up reminders in both cases. Explains how such scenarios reveal data elements, decision logic, functional requirements and adolescent-specific considerations, illustrated in a table interpreting the adolescent case.

A business process, or process, is a set of related activities or tasks performed together to achieve the objectives of the health programme area, such 
as registration, counselling and referrals (1,16). Workflows are a visual representation of the progression of activities (tasks, events and interactions) 
that are performed within the business process (16). The workflow provides a story for the business process being diagrammed and is used to enhance 
communication and collaboration among users, stakeholders and engineers.
T

summary.text: Defines business processes and workflows for the family planning digital adaptation kit and summarizes five key processes: registration, family planning counselling, service provision, referral, and aggregate reporting and data use. Lists processes left out because they depend heavily on context, such as billing, dispensing, configuration and follow-up, and explains the standard business process notation symbols used in the diagrams. The workflows are described as roughly 80% generic, with the remainder to be completed through human-centred design and validation with the targeted personas. The section ends by introducing the core data elements component, which sets out the minimum data needed for service delivery, decision support and indicators, with a fuller data dictionary in Web Annex A.

blocks.title: Table 5. Overview of key family planning module business processes
blocks.content: The table gives an overview of the five key business processes of the family planning module (A–E: registration, family planning counselling, service provision, referral, and aggregate reporting and data use). For each process it lists the process ID, the personas involved, the objectives and the task set, starting from a defined starting point.

blocks.title: Table 6. Business process symbols used in workflows
blocks.content: The table explains the standard business process notation symbols used in the workflow diagrams, from pools and swim lanes to events, activities, flows, gateways, links and ad hoc subprocesses. For each symbol it gives its name and a description of how it is used.

Fig. 5, a swimlane diagram of key family planning processes across three lanes: Health facility, Pharmacy and Health facility management. From Start, the flow runs through A. Registration and B. FP counselling to a 'Referral needed?' decision: No leads to C. FP service provision, Yes leads to D. Referral; both then pass to Billing and Dispensing before End. Configuration, Follow-up and Aggregate reporting sit in the management lane.

Fig. 6, a swimlane workflow of the registration business process with Client and Clerk lanes in a health facility. The client arrives; the clerk gathers client details, searches for the client and checks 'Match found?': Yes leads to a 'Validate client details' subprocess (review socio-demographic data, update if needed), No leads to 'Create client record'; both end with 'Check in client' and hand off to B. Counselling. Source: adapted from PATH.

Fig. 10, a swimlane workflow of the referral business process with lanes for the client and healthcare provider at the health facility and the health-care provider at the referral health facility. After counselling, an 'Emergency referral?' decision leads either to an emergency subprocess (stabilize client and give pre-referral treatment, check if stable enough to transport, organize transport) or to identifying and contacting a referral facility; once the referral facility confirms it can accommodate, the provider gives information, discusses questions and a backup method, and the client goes to the referral facility, which receives the client for C. Service provision.

Fig. 11, a swimlane workflow of the aggregate reporting business process with lanes for facility staff, facility in charge and district health officer/staff. Facility staff check data quality, correct fixable issues, generate and check aggregate reports; if in-charge review is needed, the facility in charge reviews and either provides feedback (looping back to data checks) or submits data electronically. The district reviews submitted data and either ends the process or provides feedback to the facility.

This section provides an overview of illustrative functional and non-functional requirements that may be considered to kick-start the process of 
designing or adapting the digital tracking and decision-support system. Functional requirements describe the capabilities the system must have in order 
to meet the end-users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process. Non-functional requirements provide the general attributes and features of 
the digital system to ensure usability and overcome technical and physical constr

summary.text: Provides illustrative functional and non-functional requirements to start designing or adapting a digital tracking and decision-support system for family planning. Functional requirements are written as user stories stating the role, what is wanted and why, starting with registration needs such as urgent-case bypass, client search with at least two identifiers, duplicate avoidance and mandatory fields, with the complete set in Web Annex D. Non-functional requirements describe general system qualities, including multiple languages, usability on small screens, reliability, central configuration of business rules, and interoperability through mediators and APIs. The lists are described as not exhaustive and meant to be adapted to context and user needs, ending with synchronization across facilities even when connectivity is intermittent.

blocks.content: The table lists the non-functional requirements of the digital system, grouped by category such as security (confidentiality, authentication, audit trail and logs, user management) and system requirements (general, scalability, usability, configuration, interoperability, hardware and connectivity). Each row gives a requirement ID, its category and the requirement.

summary.text: Gives guidance for adding or amending data elements when adapting the data dictionary of the family planning digital adaptation kit, for example to match existing paper registers or local reporting needs, while keeping standard terminology codes accurate. A table explains what to record for each element, including activity and form identifiers, labels, names, definitions, data types aligned with FHIR, input options, calculations, validation, editability and whether the field is required. blocks.title: Guidance for each method
blocks.content:
This annex is intended to provide additional information that can be used for developing further decision-support logic and counselling aids. This 
information is extracted from the Family planning global handbook for providers (2018) (14).
Copper-bearing intrauterine device (Cu-IUD)
What is it?
	» The Cu-IUD is a small, flexible plastic frame with copper sleeves or wire around it. A specifically trained health-care provider inserts it into a woman’s uterus 
through her vagina and cervix.
	» Almost all types of IUDs have one or two strings, or threads, tied to them. The strings hang through th

summary.text: An annex to the family planning digital adaptation kit gives method-by-method information, drawn from the 2018 Family planning global handbook for providers, to support further decision-support logic and counselling aids. For each contraceptive, starting with the copper-bearing and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine devices, it sets out what the method is, how effective it is, who can use it and how. It also covers side-effects, known health benefits and risks, how to advise on side-effects, clinical judgement in special cases and help for continuing users. The section ends with withdrawal, described as one of the least effective methods as commonly used, with no medical restrictions and no protection against sexually transmitted infections.
